entry.title: Lye v Comcare [2026] FCA 1517
entry.content:
This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). The Tribunal had equated Mr Lye’s capacity to work full-time usual hours in administrative duties with an ability to earn his normal weekly earnings, reducing compensation to zero. The Court found legal error and, by consent, set aside the decision and remitted the matter for redetermination.

Key holding: Under s 19(2) of the SRC Act, the Tribunal must separately assess the amount per week the employee is able to earn in suitable employment and use that to determine the reduction to NWE; merely equating capacity for normal hours with NWE is legal error.

In its reasons at [40], the Tribunal failed to address the amount per week (if any) that the applicant was able to earn in suitable employment during the relevant periods (i.e., the fourth question). As a result of the above failure, the Tribunal failed properly to address the amount (if any) by which the applicant's NWE should be reduced in order to determine the amount of compensation that he is entitled to receive (i.e., the sixth question).

entry.title: Mohamedali v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1531
entry.content:
The Federal Court allowed a consent judicial review application concerning a decision by the Assistant Minister under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to cancel the applicant’s visa. The Assistant Minister conceded jurisdictional error because he failed to consider an updated psychologist’s report that was constructively before him and relevant to the applicant’s risk of reoffending. The Court made orders quashing the cancellation decision.

Key holding: A s 501BA decision is affected by jurisdictional error if the Minister fails to properly consider material constructively before him that is relevant to the risk the applicant poses to the Australian community and the national interest.

Accordingly, the Assistant Minister accepts that his decision was affected by jurisdictional error as a result of his failure to properly consider the risk the applicant posed to the Australian community.

entry.title: Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1520
entry.content:
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.

Key holding: Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

entry.title: CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency and NGVL (Guidance and Appeals Panel) [2026] ARTA 2328
entry.content:
The Guidance and Appeals Panel reviewed an ART decision that had found funding for an Orangutan Plus Funky Monkey Bars Frame and accessories to be a reasonable and necessary NDIS support for NGVL, a child with Autism and ADHD. The Panel focused on whether the equipment was “standard indoor or outdoor play equipment” excluded by item 4(p) of Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules.

Key holding: Standard outdoor play equipment falling within item 4(p) of Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules is not an NDIS support and cannot be funded unless it is modified or adapted to address the participant’s functional impairments.

For the reasons given below, the Panel concludes that the Funky Monkey Bars Frame and accessories are 'standard...outdoor play equipment' and are therefore an excluded support under item 4(p) in Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules. On this basis it cannot be included for funding in NGVL's SOPS.

entry.title: Jaworski v Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand (No 2) [2026] NSWCA 213
entry.content:
Mr Jaworski sought to set aside or vary the Court of Appeal’s earlier leave judgment under UCPR r 36.16, and CA ANZ sought gross sum costs. The Court dismissed the reopening application and fixed costs at $30,000 for the leave/recusal application and $6,000 for CA ANZ’s notice of motion. The dispute concerned alleged errors, bias/prejudgment and costs in ongoing litigation involving CA ANZ.

Key holding: Under UCPR r 36.16, reopening requires some error in the court's reasoning due to misapprehension of fact or law that is not solely attributable to the applicant's neglect or default.

What is required to be established on an application under r 36.16 is some error in the court's reasoning because of a misapprehension of the facts or misapprehension of the relevant law; and that this misapprehension cannot be attributed solely to the neglect or default of the party seeking the rehearing.

entry.title: South Australian Commission for Catholic Schools Inc and Secretary, Department of Education (Guidance and Appeals Panel) [2026] ARTA 2304
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed 2024 Commonwealth recurrent funding determinations for 84 non-government Catholic schools in South Australia. It unanimously held that mid-year reception students who began in term 3 2024 were “primary students” because reception was the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1. A majority then held those students did not have a pattern of regular attendance at school or school generally during 2024, so they failed reg 9B(1)(c) and were ineligible unless the Minister included them under reg 9B(3).

Key holding: Reception undertaken by mid-year reception students is the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1, so those students are primary students in that calendar year.

Giving the phrases to which I have already referred their natural meaning, the logical conclusion is that the 2024 mid-year reception students were in the year of schooling in a course of primary education that was immediately before year 1. It follows that, in 2024, those students were in the foundation year of schooling, were receiving primary education and were therefore primary students at their school.

entry.title: Tran and Australian Skills Quality Authority [2026] ARTA 2300
entry.content:
Mr Tran sought review of ASQA’s decision to cancel his Certificate III in Carpentry, obtained via RPL from Kingsway, a deregistered RTO. Although the Tribunal found the s 56(1)(a) ground was established because Kingsway did not provide or arrange the necessary assessment, it exercised the discretion not to cancel in exceptional circumstances. The cancellation decision was set aside and the qualification is to be treated as a valid VET RPL qualification.

Key holding: Even when the s 56(1)(a) ground is established, the Tribunal may exercise the s 56(1) discretion not to cancel a VET qualification in exceptional circumstances, including clear lack of applicant fault, misleading RTO conduct, extensive genuine industry experience, and a public interest that does not require cancellation.

The Tribunal is satisfied that the discretion under subsection 56(1) of the NVR Act not to cancel the Qualification can be safely and appropriately exercised in the exceptional circumstances of this case. That discretion may be exercised consistent with the public interest, given that Mr Tran possesses the requisite training, skills and work experience to have been awarded the Qualification on an RPL basis.

entry.title: Niven and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2274
entry.content:
This was a merits review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Niven’s Class TY Subclass 444 Special Category (Temporary) visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the applicant did not pass the character test but accepted there was another reason to revoke the cancellation, set aside the delegate’s decision, and substituted a decision revoking the cancellation.

Key holding: Under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), where an applicant fails the character test, the Tribunal may revoke mandatory cancellation if satisfied there is another reason, applying Direction no. 110.

Section 501CA(4) states that the Minister may revoke the original decision if: (a) the person makes representations in accordance with the invitation; and (b) the Minister is satisfied: (i) that the person passes the character test (as defined by s 501); or (ii) that there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

entry.title: Bennett and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2276
entry.content:
_Bennett and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS)_ [2026] ARTA 2276 concerned an NDIS participant with cerebral palsy and chronic lower-limb wounds seeking review of decisions varying his statement of participant supports, particularly funding for wound-care and continence consumables. The Tribunal applied the post-2024 NDIS support framework and set aside the decision under review.

Key holding: For a requested support to qualify as an NDIS support under s 34(1)(f), it must fall within a Schedule 1 category and must not fall within an excluded Schedule 2 category.

... for a support to be a 'NDIS support' within the meaning of s 34(1)(f), the requested support must: (a) fall within one of the categories in Schedule 1; and (b) not fall within one of the categories in Schedule 2.

entry.title: Upson and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2275
entry.content:
In Upson and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2275, a 31-year-old New Zealand citizen who has lived in Australia since infancy had his special category visa mandatorily cancelled under s 501(3A) after being sentenced to 7 years 6 months for serious drug offences. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, but the Administrative Review Tribunal set that decision aside and substituted revocation after finding “another reason” under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii).

Key holding: Under Direction no. 110, whether a non-citizen poses an “unacceptable risk” is a distinct evaluative conclusion reached by balancing the likelihood and potential harm of future offending, not merely the likelihood of re-offending.

The concept of 'risk', and whether it is 'unacceptable', under cl 8.1.2(1) of the Direction is not the same thing as the 'likelihood of the non-citizen engaging in further criminal or other serious conduct'.[25]

entry.title: Al-Hajj and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2318
entry.content:
Mr Al-Hajj sought review of the NDIA’s decision about the statement of participant supports in his NDIS plan, contending for 24/7 1:1 support worker assistance and weekly psychology. The ART considered whether those supports were reasonable and necessary under s 34(1) of the NDIS Act and related rules. It set aside the decisions and remitted the matter with orders for 3 hours/day daily personal activities, 2 hours/day community participation, and 30 hours of psychology.

Key holding: Under s 34(1)(aa) of the NDIS Act, a support must be necessary to address needs arising directly from an impairment for which the participant meets the disability or early intervention requirements.

What follows from the above determination is that for the purposes of s 34(1)(aa), the supports sought on review must be necessary to address needs of Mr Al-Hajj arising directly from his psychosocial impairments.

entry.title: Nyagua and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2298
entry.content:
This Tribunal review concerns the mandatory cancellation of Ms Nyagua’s Resident Return (Subclass 155) visa after her conviction for importing a marketable quantity of a border-controlled drug. Although she failed the character test, the Tribunal found another reason to revoke the cancellation. The decision under review was set aside and the visa cancellation revoked under s 501CA(4).

Key holding: Where a non-citizen fails the character test after mandatory visa cancellation, the Tribunal may revoke cancellation under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) if satisfied there is another reason, exercising the discretion in accordance with the applicable ministerial direction.

Section 501CA(4)(b)(ii) of the Act requires the Tribunal to consider if there is another reason why the discretion should be exercised to revoke the original decision. In exercising this discretion, the Tribunal must have regard to the Direction (s 499(2A)).

entry.title: Majak and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2277
entry.content:
Majak sought review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his Class XB Subclass 202 visa under s 501(3A) after serious assault convictions. The Tribunal accepted he failed the character test but found “another reason” to revoke under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), principally the best interests of his infant daughter and the extreme impediments if removed to South Sudan. It set aside the delegate’s decision and substituted revocation.

Key holding: Where the Tribunal is satisfied on the evidence that another reason exists, it should set aside the non-revocation decision and substitute revocation under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii).

Having reached this conclusion, I find that there is 'another reason' for the revocation of the cancellation decision for the purposes of section 501CA(4)(b)(ii) of the Act. Accordingly, it is appropriate for me to set aside the decision under review and substitute decision that the cancellation decision be revoked.

entry.title: FPXJ and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2321
entry.content:
The Applicant, FPXJ, sought an extension of time to bring second review applications in the Administrative Review Tribunal against two AAT first review decisions dated 19 August 2019 and 29 January 2020 concerning disability support pension debts. The Tribunal rejected his procedural and bias arguments and refused the extension. It found the delay exceeded six years, was not fully explained, and that reopening settled matters would prejudice the Respondent and wider public, with no practical utility in the substantive review.

Key holding: Under s 19 of the ART Act, the Tribunal may refuse an extension of time where significant delay, prejudice and lack of practical utility mean it is not reasonable in all the circumstances to extend time.

Given this, and given the prejudice to the Respondent and to the wider public if an extension of time is granted, the Tribunal has decided that it is not reasonable in all of the circumstances to extend time for the Applicant to make second review applications. The extension of time applications are refused by the Tribunal.

entry.title: ROBB and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2279
entry.content:
The Tribunal affirmed a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Robb’s subclass 155 visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Mr Robb accepted he failed the character test because of a substantial criminal record, and the Tribunal found the protection of the Australian community, family violence and community expectations outweighed his ties and rehabilitation claims. The case is a fact-specific Direction No. 110 review.

Key holding: Where an applicant fails the character test, the Tribunal can revoke a mandatory visa cancellation only if satisfied under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) that there is another reason, assessed through Direction No. 110.

The statutory power to revoke will only be enlivened if there is 'another reason' why the Cancellation Decision should be revoked.

entry.title: 2104609 (Refugee) [2026] ARTA 2306
entry.content:
In 2104609 (Refugee) [2026] ARTA 2306, the Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of protection visas to Indian nationals in an interfaith/inter-caste marriage who claimed family and honour-based violence in Punjab. The delegate refused under s 65 because the applicants were not refugees and did not meet complementary protection. The Tribunal set aside the refusal and remitted the matter with a direction that the applicants meet s 36(2)(aa) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth).

Key holding: A protection visa may be granted on complementary protection grounds where the refugee criterion is not met, if removal creates a real risk of significant harm as a necessary and foreseeable consequence.

The issues in this case are whether the applicants have a well-founded fear of being persecuted in India for one or more of the five reasons set out, and, if not, whether there are substantial grounds for believing that, as a necessary and foreseeable consequence of the applicant being removed from Australia to India there is a real risk that they will suffer significant harm.

entry.title: Yerburgh and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security) [2026] ARTA 2291
entry.content:
In Yerburgh and Secretary, Department of Social Services [2026] ARTA 2291, the Tribunal reviewed a decision reducing Mrs Yerburgh’s age pension by assessing notional income from a farm treated as an unrealisable asset. The Tribunal set aside the decision and remitted the rate for reassessment from 11 October 2024 on the basis that the relevant income amount was her actual annual ordinary income from the farm, not a commercial lease value.

Key holding: Where an unrealisable farm is already being worked commercially to full capacity, the amount reasonably expected from a purely commercial application under s 1130(5)(b) is the actual income from current operations, and the s 1130(5) notional rate is the lesser of that amount and 2.5% of the farm's value.

However, having heard from Mrs Yerburgh, the Tribunal is satisfied that the farm is currently being operated commercially to its full capacity. As such, the Tribunal finds that what Mrs Yerburgh could reasonably be expected to obtain from a purely commercial application of the farm is the income that is actually being generated from its current operations, not some alternative higher commercial lease figure as adopted by Centrelink.

entry.title: Kirby and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security) [2026] ARTA 2292
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a Centrelink decision raising a $4,109.18 newstart allowance debt against Mr Kirby for 30 November 2018 to 1 April 2019 due to undeclared employment income. The Tribunal set aside the decision and remitted the matter because Centrelink’s earlier income apportionment was not the method required under s 1117D(9) of the Social Security Act 1991. Any recalculated overpayment remains a Commonwealth debt and recovery was not waived.

Key holding: Where pre-7 December 2020 Division 3 work income is reviewed and neither the entitlement period in which it was earned nor the payroll period can be identified, it must be assessed under s 1117D(9) in the entitlement period in which it was received.

This means that the third approach in subsection 1117D(9) must be used so that [Mr Kirby's] wages are to be assessed on each day of the newstart allowance entitlement period in which he received the income.

entry.title: Tambling and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security) [2026] ARTA 2295
entry.content:
Ms Tambling was granted Disability Support Pension from 21 August 2023, but Centrelink calculated her rate using an allegedly incorrect gifting/assets assessment. On internal review, the ARO found she had been underpaid $31,904.71, but paid only $25,191.54 due to date-of-effect limits under s 109 of the Social Security (Administration) Act 1999 (Cth). The Tribunal found the remaining arrears were payable and set aside the review decision.

Key holding: Where a person is given notice of a decision and requests review within 13 weeks, a favourable determination on review takes effect from the date of the original decision.

Subsection 109(1) provides that if a person is given notice of a decision, and they request a review within 13 weeks after the date the notice is given, the favourable determination takes effect on the date the original decision took effect.

entry.title: 2407106 (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2270
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of a Student (Temporary) (Class TU) visa because a bogus bank document had supported the applicant’s earlier Temporary Activity visa. The Tribunal accepted the document was bogus but found the applicant was unaware of it and neither complicit in nor recklessly indifferent to her coach’s or agent’s conduct. It set aside the refusal and remitted the matter with a direction that PIC 4020 is met for cl 500.217(1).

Key holding: For PIC 4020(1), where a third party supplies a bogus document, an applicant may be taken to have caused it to be given if complicit in, or recklessly indifferent to, that third party’s unlawful or dishonest conduct.

If the applicant is complicit in the provision of false information or 'indifferent' to a third party acting unlawfully or dishonestly, it can be said that the applicant caused it to be given.

entry.title: 2004494 (Refugee) [2026] ARTA 2303
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed the refusal of a Protection (Class XA) Subclass 866 visa for a young girl born in Australia to Malaysian citizen parents. It accepted that she is stateless, born out of wedlock, and unable to register her birth or readily obtain Malaysian citizenship. The Tribunal found she faces a real chance of serious harm in Malaysia and remitted the matter with a direction that she satisfies s 36(2)(a).

Key holding: A stateless child born out of wedlock in Malaysia may meet the refugee criterion where discriminatory citizenship and registration laws, combined with social stigma, cause serious harm for reasons of nationality and membership of a particular social group, without effective state protection.

I find that the applicant faces a real chance of serious harm for the essential and significant reasons of her nationality, or lack thereof, and because of her membership of the particular social group 'children born out of wedlock'. This characteristic is an innate or immutable characteristic, and it is not a fear of persecution.

entry.title: 2215119 (Refugee) [2026] ARTA 2305
entry.content:
The ART reviewed a delegate’s refusal of protection visas to a Malaysian family of Indian Malay Roman Catholics. The Tribunal accepted their evidence of racial and religious harassment/discrimination, rejected their loan-shark claims for lack of evidence, and found each applicant met the refugee criterion. It set aside the delegate’s decisions and remitted the matter for reconsideration.

Key holding: Serious, country-wide discrimination or harassment based on race or religion, coupled with unavailable state protection, can amount to persecution under the refugee criterion, and an applicant need not modify their behaviour to avoid it.

entry.title: 2105145 (Refugee) [2026] ARTA 2314
entry.content:
The ARTA reviewed a delegate’s refusal of Class XA Subclass 866 protection visas to an Indian mother and her two daughters. The Tribunal accepted that the first applicant, a divorced single mother, faced a real chance of serious harm in India as a member of a particular social group of women/single divorced women. It set aside the refusal and remitted the applications for reconsideration.

Key holding: A non-citizen single divorced woman from India may be a refugee where country information shows a real chance of serious harm from the broader community for the essential and significant reason of her profile as a single divorced woman.

For the reasons discussed, the Tribunal is satisfied that the applicant has a real chance of serious harm in the reasonably foreseeable future for the essential and significant reason of her profile as a single, divorced woman, if she returned to India.

entry.title: 2006580 (Refugee) [2026] ARTA 2271
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of a subclass 866 protection visa to an Iranian citizen who claims to have converted from Islam to Christianity in Australia. It accepted his core claims, found Iran would not protect him as a Christian convert, set aside the refusal and remitted the matter for reconsideration under s 36(2)(a) of the Migration Act.

Key holding: Where an applicant engages in religious conduct in Australia after arrival, s 5J(6) requires that conduct to be disregarded for the refugee assessment unless the applicant proves it was not done to strengthen the refugee claim; a genuine, sustained conversion supported by evidence can satisfy that requirement.

Section 5J(6) provides that any conduct engaged in by a person in Australia must be disregarded in determining whether the person has a well-founded fear of being persecuted for reasons of race, religion, nationality, or membership of a particular social group or political opinion, unless the person satisfies the decision maker that he or she engaged in the conduct otherwise than for the purpose of strengthening the claim to be a refugee.

entry.title: Julie Rawlins v Coca Cola Europacific Partners Australia Pty Ltd [2026] VCC 341 (30 March 2026)
entry.content:
Julie Rawlins, a Business Development Executive for Coca-Cola Europacific Partners, suffered a right thumb injury on 23 April 2020 while performing "facing up" (rotating bottles to face forward) duties at a retail store. A jury found the defendant negligent but rejected her statutory duty claim. entry.title: Goncalves De Sa (Migration) [2024] AATA 3350
entry.content:
The Tribunal affirmed refusal of Employer Nomination (Permanent) (Class EN) Subclass 186 visas in the Temporary Residence Transition stream because the primary applicant, a chef, could not demonstrate competent English at the time of application. Although he spoke English well at hearing and had substantial culinary experience, his IELTS results and Portuguese passport did not meet the prescribed criteria, and the Tribunal had no discretion.

Key holding: For a Subclass 186 TRT visa, competent English must be established at the time of application through a specified test score or specified passport, failing which cl 186.222(a) is not satisfied and the Tribunal has no discretion.

Since neither 1.15C(1) nor 1.15C(2) are satisfied, 1.15C is not satisfied. As 1.15C is not satisfied, the Tribunal finds the applicant did not have competent English at the time of lodging the visa application, and therefore does not satisfy 186.222(a).
